clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive alpha-dystroglycanopathy caused by mutations in FKTN (fukutin); a founder mutation makes it one of the commonest muscular dystrophies in Japan.
Defined by a triad of congenital muscular dystrophy, type II (cobblestone) lissencephaly and ocular abnormalities.
Generalised hypotonia and weakness are present from birth or early infancy, with poor motor development, joint contractures and calf pseudohypertrophy.
Intellectual disability and seizures are characteristic, distinguishing it from many other congenital muscular dystrophies.
Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated.
Brain MRI shows cobblestone cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts and polymicrogyria, brainstem hypoplasia and white-matter signal change.
Dilated cardiomyopathy tends to develop in the second decade and respiratory insufficiency is common, so cardiac and respiratory surveillance is essential.
It sits on a severity spectrum with muscle-eye-brain disease and the most severe Walker-Warburg syndrome.
reference.pathophysiology: Fukutin is a ribitol-phosphate transferase required for the O-mannosyl glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. When this glycosylation is deficient, alpha-dystroglycan can no longer bind laminin and other extracellular matrix ligands, so the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex that anchors the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the basal lamina is disrupted, causing membrane fragility and a dystrophic myopathy. The same defect weakens the glia limitans and its basement membrane in the developing brain, allowing neurons to overmigrate through breaches in the pial surface to produce the cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly, and it disrupts retinal lamination, which together account for the combined muscle, brain and eye phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Merosin (laminin alpha-2, LAMA2)-deficient congenital muscular dystrophy
Other dystroglycanopathies (POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, FKRP, LARGE)
Congenital myopathies and congenital myotonic dystrophy
Spinal muscular atrophy and other causes of the floppy infant
Peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan
Brain MRI for cortical malformation and cerebellar and brainstem changes
Respiratory function testing and sleep studies
redFlags: Deteriorating cardiac function from dilated cardiomyopathy
Prolonged or recurrent seizures progressing to status epilepticus
Progressive feeding difficulty and failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: The condition is severe: most children achieve only limited motor milestones and never walk independently, and survival is frequently limited to the first or second decade owing to respiratory and cardiac complications.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the floppy infant as spinal muscular atrophy or non-specific hypotonia
Neglecting cardiac and respiratory surveillance for later-onset cardiomyopathy and hypoventilation
Failing to place the child within the dystroglycanopathy spectrum, delaying genetic counselling
Overlooking the associated brain malformation when weakness dominates the presentation
management: No curative therapy is available; management is supportive and multidisciplinary
Physiotherapy, stretching and orthoses to manage contractures and maintain posture and seating
Respiratory surveillance with non-invasive ventilation for progressive respiratory insufficiency
Cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and heart-failure therapy for dilated cardiomyopathy
Antiepileptic drugs for seizures with EEG guidance
Developmental, educational and nutritional support including safe feeding and gastrostomy where needed
Anticipatory and palliative care given the limited prognosis
Genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive FKTN disorder
